extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and writers interested in horror fiction (genre overview and creative-writing guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of the horror-fiction genre: definitions, history, subgenres, and the key characteristics and thematic/psychological effects that make horror effective for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended emotional response: disturb, frighten, or scare
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror is a genre of speculative fiction that is intended to disturb, frighten, or scare an audience. J. A. Cuddon defined the horror story as 'a piece of fiction in prose of variable length ... which shocks, or even frightens the reader, or perhaps induces a feeling of repulsion or loathing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary evaluative criterion for horror is whether the work produces those emotional reactions in readers. Examples and historic exemplars (Dracula, Frankenstein) are cited as works that achieve shock, fright, or repulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eerie and frightening atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror intends to create an eerie and frightening atmosphere for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atmosphere is pivotal: setting, mood, sensory detail and pacing contribute to an unsettling tone. The page links atmosphere to the genre's purpose and to other criteria (fear, dread, terror) and notes that threats in the fiction often build that atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threats should reflect broader cultural anxieties / use of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: The threats present in horror fiction often reflect broader cultural anxieties. Menacing villains and monsters can often be seen as metaphors for the fears incarnate of a society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers can make monsters/menaces resonate by tying them to social, political, sexual, or cultural fears (example: Dracula's vampirism as a metaphor for sexuality and class). This is both a thematic quality and an evaluative dimension: effective horror often has metaphorical depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear of the unknown (evoke dread)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lovecraft: 'The oldest and strongest emotion of mankind is fear, and the oldest and strongest kind of fear is fear of the unknown.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common mechanism in horror is to exploit uncertainty and the unknown; stories that successfully unsettle readers often withhold explanation or reveal only gradually, cultivating dread and cosmic or existential unease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Menace must be threatening (truly menacing, life-destroying)
rubrics_metrics.description: Darrell Schweitzer: 'the true horror story requires a sense of evil... the menaces must be truly menacing, life-destroying, and antithetical to happiness.' Noël Carroll likewise requires a menace that is threatening—physically, psychologically, socially, morally, spiritually, or some combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective horror presents stakes that genuinely imperil characters' lives, sanity, social standing, or moral order. Vague or trivial threats reduce emotional impact; strong horror escalates consequences and danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Menace must be impure (violate cultural/categorical schemes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Noël Carroll: a menace must be impure — that which 'violates the generally accepted schemes of cultural categorization.' 'We consider impure that which is categorically contradictory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antagonists or horrors that blur categories (human/nonhuman, living/dead, natural/supernatural, moral/immoral) create cognitive and affective dissonance that intensifies horror. Writers can design monsters or situations that defy straightforward classification to unsettle readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terror versus horror distinction (temporal and affective difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ann Radcliffe's distinction: 'terror' is a feeling of dread that takes place before an event happens, whereas 'horror' is a feeling of revulsion or disgust after an event has happened. Radcliffe: terror 'expands the soul and awakens the faculties to a high degree of life,' horror 'freezes and nearly annihilates them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft choices depend on whether the work aims to build anticipatory dread (terror) or to shock and disgust with graphic or overwhelming revelation (horror). Effective authors manipulate both modes depending on desired effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best horror intends to challenge complacency and provoke thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Elizabeth Barrette: while some horror intends to shock and disgust, 'the best horror intends to rattle our cages and shake us out of our complacency. It makes us think, forces us to confront ideas we might rather ignore, and challenges preconceptions of all kinds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond eliciting fear, effective horror often has an intellectual or ethical edge: it prompts reflection, critique, or re-evaluation of assumptions. Evaluations may reward works that combine visceral effect with conceptual challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of setting and Gothic elements as genre conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gothic tradition provided many conventions (gloomy castles, medieval trappings, resourceful female threatened in a castle) that shaped later horror. Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto initiated Gothic motifs widely reused in horror fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting and genre-specific motifs (decaying architecture, isolation, inherited curses) are tools to create dread and atmosphere. Critics and editors may assess how well an author uses or reinvents these conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre distinctions and associated techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror is often divided into sub-genres such as psychological horror and supernatural horror; the article also references cosmic horror, zombie/apocalyptic tales, slasher/splatter, dark fantasy, weird fiction, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different subgenres employ different mechanisms: psychological horror emphasizes character interiority and mental dread; supernatural horror emphasizes otherworldly forces; cosmic horror emphasizes insignificance and incomprehensible forces. Evaluation should consider subgenre expectations and how effectively the work meets or subverts them.
